provenance.description: The Cleveland Museum of Art, Cleveland, Ohio
(Sloan & Roman, Inc., New York, NY, sold to the Cleveland Museum of Art)
(The Terry DeLapp Gallery, Los Angeles, CA, sold to Sloan & Roman)1
footnotes: 1 A hand-typed fact sheet (in CMA curatorial file) presumably produced at the time of the painting’s acquisition in 1970 lists a “John Johnson” in the provenance following the Terry DeLapp Gallery.  While it is possible that Johnson, who appears to have owned or bought/sold at least one other Gifford painting, acted as an intermediary or agent in the sale of the painting, DeLapp emphatically states that he sold the painting directly to Sloan & Roman.

provenance.description: (T. Gilbert Brouillette [1906-1970], Staten Island, NY, sold to the Terry DeLapp Gallery) 1
footnotes: 1 Although Brouillette was a collector as well as a dealer, Terry DeLapp, to whom Brouillette sold the painting, indicates Brouillette acted as a dealer in the sale of this painting.  Brouillette’s papers at the Archives of American Art contain no reference to the painting.

provenance.description: James M. Hartshorne [d. 1887?], New York, NY?

data.did_you_know: Gifford considered this painting to be one of his finest creations.
data.description: Gifford’s view of Mount Hayes in New Hampshire records human intrusion into a remote landscape. On the left riverbank a log cabin stands amid a recently cleared patch of land with several tree stumps, while figures in its doorway greet a man who has arrived with a canoe of supplies.
